content.p: The Diablos Motorcycle Club is a red-and-yellow club that began in Thailand in 1999 and now has chapters in 15 countries, according to a 2023 report by the news outlet ScandAsia. News reports in Sweden and Finland describe it as a support club of the Bandidos, the larger motorcycle club. Finland's Keskusrikospoliisi (central criminal police) classifies both clubs as criminal organisations.

Members of the club tell a different story. The British president of the Khon Kaen chapter in Thailand told ScandAsia that the Diablos are "just a bunch of guys who loves bikes" and that the odd bad member shows up in any organisation. The record that can be checked in newspapers and official notices is more mixed. It contains police raids in Malmö, a debt-collection case in Finland that ended in eight convictions, a ban on one chapter in Germany, and an episode in Victoria, Australia, in which the Diablos clubhouse became the target of a Hells Angels show of force. Each of these involved individuals, and none of it shows what every member of the club does.

Large outlaw clubs rarely stand alone. Sweden's public broadcaster SVT explained in 2006 that the main gangs were setting up support clubs in the countryside, where weapons and drugs were easier to hide and the groups harder to reach. A national police official, Peter Tjäder of Rikskriminalpolisen, called the trend very worrying. SVT described the Bandidos as an international hierarchy in which every chapter, aspirant club and support club paid fees to the country's main chapter.

Reports in Sweden and Finland place the Diablos in that structure. Kvällsposten called the Malmö club a support group for the Bandidos, and Kaleva wrote in 2014 that Diablos is part of the Bandidos. How closely the clubs are tied in practice is something outsiders rely on police to describe. The Diablos' own accounts stress friendship. The history of the chapter in Belgium, for instance, records how its members went from the Smokers, through riding with the Compadres patch, to wearing Diablos colours.

ScandAsia traced the club to Thailand in 1999 and said that around 80 percent of its members there are Thai. The Khon Kaen chapter it visited was an exception: six members, all foreign, including a Swedish vice president and a British president who with his wife owns the restaurant above which the clubhouse sits. The members described how recruits are chosen. "You don't ask to be a member of Diablos, you are being asked to join," the president said, adding that joining is a long process. They said that chapter does charity work, such as delivering presents to orphanages at Christmas.

The chapter in Belgium wrote its own history. Six members of a club called the Smokers travelled to a Bandidos party in Luxemburg on 30 March 2002, where they met the Compadres MC of Rumst. Compadres later became the Bandidos' chapter in Belgium. In March 2003 the Smokers received full patches from the president of the Bandidos in Belgium, and at a Bandidos national run they were given a badge reading "I SUPPORT BANDIDOS MC WORLDWIDE". After two years of riding with the Compadres patch they decided to join what they called the red and gold family. On 16 October 2004, at an anniversary party at the Compadres clubhouse and with Diablos delegations from Germany and Sweden present, they received their full Diablos colours. The history also records good contacts with the Diablos in Wetzlar.
content.h2: Malmö: a clubhouse under repeated police attention
content.p: The Swedish chapter appears in the news mainly through police operations. ScandAsia, summarising the record, wrote that in 2002 two Diablos members were arrested at the Malmö clubhouse after an assault at a nightclub that left three people injured. In 2006 police raided the same clubhouse and seized amphetamine, it said, and the president of the Malmö chapter was later sentenced to eight months in prison for firearms possession.

Kvällsposten, reporting a new raid in June 2007, gave more detail on that earlier operation. On 26 February 2006, it wrote, police searched the club's premises and found equipment for handling amphetamine. At the same time, officers searching the home of the club's 48-year-old leader found several loaded firearms, among them two loaded automatic pistols kept near his bed. The paper called the Diablos a support group for the Bandidos.

The 2007 raid came on 27 June, when customs officers and riot police entered the clubhouse on Fortunavägen. They were looking for a wanted man born in 1985 who was suspected of serious drug smuggling. He was arrested at the premises, along with five others in their twenties suspected of drug offences, and about 50 grams of cannabis was seized. A customs duty officer said the case had been long in the making and followed extended cooperation between Malmö police and customs. ScandAsia also reported that eight members of the Malmö chapter were arrested in 2007 after police found weapons and narcotics in another raid. A British chapter president in Thailand, asked about the club's reputation, said "there will always be someone doing something naughty" in any organisation.
content.h2: Oulu and Varkaus: the cases in Finland
content.p: In September 2011 Kaleva quoted a Keskusrikospoliisi chief in Oulu saying police were watching two motorcycle clubs in the city suspected of involvement in crime, the Hells Angels and the Bandidos-linked Diablos. Police considered such clubs part of organised crime. They counted about 80 organised criminal groups in Finland with about a thousand members.

On 18 October 2011 police searched the premises of what Kaleva called Diablos MC Prospect CH Oulu, a group that was seeking full membership. The only person inside was the local leader, who was taken into custody. Police said little. Kaleva reported the following May that police had searched the premises because of a serious crime suspected to have happened there.

The next spring a shooting in an Oulu restaurant put the club in the headlines again. In the small hours of Friday 25 May 2012, a man was shot and wounded at the restaurant Tivoli. A 19-year-old arrested nearby was, according to preliminary police information, linked to the Diablos, though a police investigator told Kaleva he was not wearing a vest. At trial the young man, then 20, was charged with attempted manslaughter, assault and a firearms offence. He admitted the firearms charge and the earlier punches but denied intent to kill. Police said he was a Diablos member. He denied that, telling investigators he was not yet a member and had been allowed to be around the club with all members' approval. The victim's girlfriend said that her partner had been asked to join the Diablos and refused, and that members then began to threaten him. The same police inquiry, however, found no evidence that the club as an organisation had anything to do with the shooting.

In September 2012 the district court sentenced Timothy Stuart Robinson to four and a half years in prison for aggravated assault, aggravated robbery, assault and a firearms offence. Part of the case was a robbery earlier in May in which two men took a victim to a parking area and beat him with a bat and an iron pipe; the other man received two years and eight months. The sentence did not change on appeal in April 2013, although the court of appeal raised one victim's compensation for post-traumatic stress to 3,000 euros. Kaleva noted that police say Robinson has links to Diablos MC.

In 2014 the Varkaus chapter was named in a wider Oulu case. According to the prosecutor and later the district court, Diablos MC Varkaus asked the Oulu section of the Bandidos to collect a debt. Both described the debt as legally valid. The prosecutor said the task went to the Oulu leader, who ordered two others to carry it out. A man was forced into a car under threat of a telescopic baton and driven to a cash machine; unable to withdraw what was needed, he was made to make two transfers totalling 2,200 euros, of which, said the prosecutor, 1,000 euros went to Diablos MC Warkaus. The two collectors later demanded another 640 euros as a collection fee. The court found that 1,640 euros had been taken from the victim that the collectors had no right to.

In January 2015 Oulu district court sentenced eight men over the debt collection. One received one year and eleven months in prison for extortion and an aggravated drug offence, another a year's suspended sentence for extortion, one a fine for aiding extortion, and five were punished for inciting it with fines or suspended terms. The court said several sentences were influenced by earlier convictions and by membership of an organisation classified as a criminal organisation, and that those sentenced included members of the Bandidos' Oulu leadership. The same wider case involved a separate brutal robbery with three prison sentences of about three to nearly four years. That robbery was not described as a Diablos matter, and in all 16 people were sentenced across the case.

The Varkaus clubhouse also attracted political attention. In April 2012 MTV Uutiset relayed a report by an evening newspaper, abbreviated IL, which cited police sources saying that Teuvo Hakkarainen, a Finns Party member of parliament, had been seen at the Diablos clubhouse in Varkaus around the turn of the year, and that a local Finns Party politician was a visible member of the club. Hakkarainen had already explained a February visit to Bandidos premises by saying he was lured there from a restaurant to carry on the evening and did not at first know whose premises they were.

In Nordrhein-Westfalen the state interior ministry issued an order on 23 April 2012 prohibiting the Bandidos MC Chapter Aachen and its sub-organisations. The order named the Chicanos chapters of Aachen, Alsdorf and Düren, the X-Team MC Aachen and Diablos MC Heinsberg. It found that the club's purpose and activities ran contrary to criminal law, dissolved the groups, banned the use of their emblems and ordered their assets seized. It was published in the state's official gazette in December 2012.

In March 2017 a nationwide ban on displaying the badges of eight rocker groups, among them the Diablos, came into force. Nordrhein-Westfalen's interior minister, Ralf Jäger, said he would enforce it consistently, calling the patches an expression of this scene's contempt for the state. The ministry counted 48 chapters of the eight groups in the state, with about 1,500 members in all.

In Australia the Diablos appear less as suspects than as the target of a rival gang. On the night of 1 March 2013 about 200 bikers, gathered at the direction of the Hells Angels, walked from the Satans Soldiers clubhouse to the nearby Melton clubhouse of the Diablos, which the Border Mail described as associated with the Bandidos. The hearing of an appeal over cancelled firearms licences was told that this was a "run through". Police alleged the group forced the occupants against a wall, took their driver's licences and photographed them. The Sydney Morning Herald, reporting evidence from Detective Senior Sergeant Wayne Cheesman, said the girlfriends of Diablos members had their details taken as a threat against talking to police, that a Diablo was bashed, and that a Hells Angels member was seen with a machine gun.

About half an hour later a convoy of Bandidos arrived. According to the Sydney Morning Herald, video footage shows members of the Hells Angels group ambushing the convoy in cars of their own, ramming Mitchell's car and firing. Toby Mitchell, then the Bandidos' Australasian sergeant-at-arms, was shot in the right arm, and another Bandido was lightly wounded. The Border Mail reported more than 30 rounds fired. Mitchell, who had survived being shot five times in 2011 and refused to help police, quit the Bandidos by November 2013, the Sydney Morning Herald reported, because of ill health it linked to two murder attempts; police confirmed he had handed in his colours. He left in good standing, the paper said. In 2019 3AW, citing the Herald Sun, reported that he had posted a photograph of himself in a Mongols T-shirt.
